title: Home from Babylon: Rebuilding Jerusalem
lead: Even seventy years of captivity do not mean that God has forgotten His people. What has lain in ruins for years can be rebuilt.
questions: What in my life has lain in ruins so long that I have stopped believing it can be rebuilt, and which stretch of wall is closest to my own house?
Do I let weeping and joy sound together in my rebuilding, or do I make myself choose one?
What matter should I start drawing the bow of prayer for right now, so that when the decisive moment comes, I am ready to loose a short arrow?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: After seventy years, ruin stops being a wound and becomes simply the way things are. And then “the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia.” Cyrus issues a decree of return, just as Jeremiah had foretold, and the temple vessels carried off by one pagan king are handed back by another. History never slipped out of God’s hands for a moment. Those who go back are “everyone whose spirit God had stirred”: they leave settled lives behind to go and live among the rubble. Hope is sometimes exactly that: not a feeling, but a move toward the ruins.

When the foundations of the new temple were laid, the old men who remembered the first one wept loudly and the young shouted for joy, until “the people could not distinguish the shouts of joy from the sound of weeping.” And no one hushed anyone. That is the sound of every real rebuilding: whoever raises a marriage, a faith, or a community out of the rubble will hear both voices inside at once, and both belong. Ninety years later Nehemiah, the king’s cupbearer, heard that Jerusalem’s walls still lay in ruins. He wept, fasted, and prayed for four months, reminding God of His promises. And when the king asked what he wanted, he “prayed to the God of heaven and answered the king.” The shortest prayer in the Bible hit its mark because it had four months of drawing the bow behind it.

The wall was then rebuilt not by professionals but by families: priests, goldsmiths, merchants, even the daughters of Shallum, each at the stretch nearest home. Great ruins are not lifted by one hero, but by many ordinary people, each at their own few yards of wall. When mockery and threats came, they worked with one hand and held a weapon in the other, and to four invitations into an ambush Nehemiah replied: “I am doing a great work and cannot come down.” There is work you do not step away from. The wall stood after fifty-two days, and the enemies “realized that this task had been accomplished by our God.” If something in your life has lain in ruins for years, it is not past its deadline. It is enough to start with one stretch of wall.

Seventy years is a whole lifetime. People who as children had watched Jerusalem burn died in Babylon as old men, and their grandchildren knew the homeland only from stories. After that long, ruin stops being a wound and becomes simply the way things are: no one remembers anymore that it could ever have been different. Today’s story is about a God whose memory is longer than ours. And about the fact that rebuilding what has lain in rubble for decades is possible; it just looks different from what we dreamed of.

sections.heading: A Pagan King’s Spirit Stirred
paragraphs: Everything begins with a sentence that sets out the theology of both of today’s books: “In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, to fulfill the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah, the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia.” Babylon, which had destroyed Jerusalem, has itself just fallen, and the new ruler of the world issues a decree: whoever belongs to the LORD’s people, “may he go to Jerusalem in Judah and build the house of the LORD, the God of Israel.” Jeremiah had foretold seventy years of captivity, and Isaiah, long before Cyrus was born, had called him by name as the one who would carry out God’s plans. Archaeology has added its own footnote: the clay Cyrus Cylinder has survived, and on it the king describes his policy of sending deported peoples home and rebuilding their temples. The grand politics of an empire turned out to be a tool in the hand of the God of a small, conquered nation. There is one more detail in this scene, and it closes the bracket of the exile: Cyrus returns the temple vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had carried off from Jerusalem. One pagan king took them; another pagan king gave them back. Through all that time, history never slipped out of God’s hands for a moment.

sections.heading: Those Whose Spirit Was Stirred
paragraphs: The decree opened the way for everyone, but the text puts it more carefully: the family heads of Judah and Benjamin, the priests and the Levites set out, “everyone whose spirit God had stirred.” Not everyone. After seventy years, Babylon was home: there were businesses there, gardens, the graves of loved ones, a whole settled life. Many stayed, and yesterday’s story of Esther showed that God did not turn His back on those who stayed. But those who got up made a decision that was crazy from every sensible point of view: to leave the prosperity of the empire and travel some six hundred miles to go and live among the rubble. Sometimes hope takes exactly this shape: not a feeling, but a move. You pack up your life and set out toward the ruins, because you have come to believe they are not the last word. Archaeology has added a surprising footnote to this return as well: excavations of settlements from the Persian period show that those coming back from exile built houses larger and sturdier than the ones from before the destruction. People who had come to live on rubble did not throw together something makeshift to wait things out. They built as if they believed in a future that would last for generations. That is how you can tell whether someone has really come back.

sections.heading: Weeping and Joy in One Voice
paragraphs: Once they have arrived and the first months have passed, the settlers lay the foundations of a new temple. The priests stand in their vestments with trumpets, the Levites with cymbals, and they sing the song Israel still sings today: “For He is good; for His loving devotion to Israel endures forever.” And then comes one of the truest scenes in the whole Bible: “But many of the older priests, Levites, and family heads who had seen the first temple wept loudly when they saw the foundation of this temple. Still, many others shouted joyfully. The people could not distinguish the shouts of joy from the sound of weeping.” The old men wept because they remembered that house and could see this one would be humbler. The young shouted for joy because for the first time in their lives they were watching something in Jerusalem begin rather than end. And no one hushed anyone. That is the sound of every real rebuilding: after years of ruin, the new is never simply the old come back. Whoever rebuilds a marriage, a faith, their health, or a community will hear both voices inside at once: grief for what is gone for good, and joy over what is beginning. The Bible says both belong. Out of just such a mix of weeping and singing, God knows how to build.

sections.heading: The Cupbearer Who Wept for Four Months
paragraphs: Ninety years later, the walls of Jerusalem still lie in ruins. The temple stands, but the city is defenseless and half empty. The news reaches the Persian court and Nehemiah, the king’s Jewish cupbearer: “The remnant who survived the exile are there in the province, in great trouble and disgrace. The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates are burned with fire.” The reaction of a high-ranking imperial official: “I sat down and wept. I mourned for days, fasting and praying before the God of heaven.” The book’s calendar reveals that about four months passed between that news and his conversation with the king. Four months of prayer from a man who could not yet do anything. The prayer preserved in the book is woven, sentence by sentence, out of the five books of Moses: Nehemiah reminds God of His own words about scattering His people for unfaithfulness and gathering those who return. He does not improvise. He prays the promises God Himself signed, and holds Him to His word. That is the strongest kind of prayer the Bible knows. Then the king notices his sadness and asks: “What is your request?” And here comes my favorite sentence in the book: “So I prayed to the God of heaven and answered the king.” Between the ruler’s question and the courtier’s answer lies the shortest prayer in the Bible, an arrow loosed in a split second. But that arrow flew true because it had four months of drawing the bow behind it. That is how prayer works for people who are suddenly handed their moment: lightning-fast on the outside, long on the inside. Nehemiah, like Esther yesterday, stood high up at a pagan court at exactly the moment his people needed someone high up.

sections.heading: Let Us Start Rebuilding
paragraphs: Nehemiah arrives in Jerusalem and at first says nothing. At night, on a donkey, he rides around the ruins, taking in the scale of the disaster before saying a word about it. Then he calls the leaders together, and instead of a lecture he gives a testimony: he tells them about “the gracious hand of my God upon me, and what the king had said to me.” The answer comes back: “Let us start rebuilding.” And “they set their hands to this good work.” Chapter 3 of the book is a long list that looks dull at first glance: who repaired which section of the wall. But the whole method of rebuilding is hidden in that list. The wall was repaired by priests and goldsmiths, perfumers and merchants, people from the surrounding towns, and even the daughters of a man named Shallum, among the few women in the Bible named as builders. Almost none of them were masons. Each one took the section nearest their own house. Throughout the chapter, like a refrain, one Hebrew verb meaning “to strengthen” comes back more than thirty times. Not “they raised it from scratch,” but “they strengthened”: they took what had survived and gave it back its strength. Rebuilding rarely starts from an empty lot. More often it starts from remnants that can still be strengthened. Great ruins are rebuilt not by the great effort of one hero, but by a hundred families, each strengthening its own piece. This is a lesson for churches too: the renewal of a community does not come through one outstanding person, but through many ordinary ones, each standing at their own few yards of wall.

sections.heading: One Hand on the Work, a Weapon in the Other
paragraphs: Rebuilding immediately draws opposition. Sanballat, the governor of Samaria, a man also known from papyri outside the Bible, first mocks, then threatens armed attack, and among the people discouragement finds its voice: “The strength of the laborer fails, and there is so much rubble that we will never be able to rebuild the wall.” Anyone who has taken on a big rebuilding knows that moment: the enthusiasm has drained away, and the rubble seems to have grown. Nehemiah answers with organization and prayer at the same time: “The laborers who carried materials worked with one hand and held a weapon with the other,” guards kept watch through the night, and no one took off their clothes. And when his enemies four times invite him to a “meeting” in the valley that is meant to cost him his life, he answers with a sentence that ought to hang over the desk of anyone doing something important: “I am doing a great work and cannot come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it to go down to you?” Not every provocation deserves an answer. Not every invitation has to be accepted. There is work you do not step away from. Nor did the danger come only from outside. Inside the besieged community the poor raised an outcry: better-off brothers were lending to them at interest, and they were pledging their fields, their vineyards, and finally their own children. Nehemiah rebuked the leaders publicly and made them give back what had been pledged, and for twelve years as governor he himself did not take the allowance due to him from taxes, so as not to add to the people’s burden. He knew that a wall of stone would not protect a city that was devouring itself from within. Rebuilding the walls and rebuilding justice had to go together, or neither of them made any sense. And the wall stands: “the wall was completed in fifty-two days.” The enemies, Nehemiah notes, “were afraid and disheartened, for they realized that this task had been accomplished by our God.” A wall built by the trembling hands of amateurs became an argument for the existence of God. And the celebration afterward was worthy of the building: two great thanksgiving choirs processed along the top of the wall in opposite directions until they met at the temple, and the joy of Jerusalem, so the record says, could be heard far away. They sang on a wall that not long before had been a heap of rubble. There is no better pulpit for a song of thanks than a rebuilt ruin.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: If something in your life has lain in ruins for years, so long that you have stopped even grieving over it, this story tells you three things. First: seventy years of ruin did not erase Jerusalem from God’s memory. Your ruin is not past its deadline either. Second: the rebuilding will begin not with a miracle but with a decision to get up and head toward the rubble, and it will sound like weeping and joy at once. Don’t be ashamed of either voice. Third: take the stretch of wall nearest your own house. Not the whole wall, just one stretch. And as a community, let us remember two things. Renewal is carried not by one hero but by many families, each at their own few yards of wall. And every good rebuilding will draw scoffers, who need no answer other than Nehemiah’s: I am doing a great work and cannot come down.
